title: APIs
goal: Explain how applications exchange requests and responses.
meaning: An API is a defined way for one application to ask another application to do something or return information. It is the connection contract—not the AI model itself.
work: A customer sends a chat message from an app. The app calls an AI API and displays the reply. If the call fails, you trace where the request stopped.
look: Request destination, method, response status, request ID and whether the request reached the intended service.
mistake: Assuming an API always means AI, or assuming HTTP 200 means the AI answer is factually correct.
example:
User → Web app → POST /api/chat → AI service
AI service → Response → Web app → User
q: What is the API's primary role here?
options: To generate the model response inside the browser
To define how systems exchange requests and responses
To store every customer conversation
why: An API defines how software communicates. It does not guarantee an AI answer's correctness.
optionReasons: The model produces the response; the API defines the communication contract.
An API defines how software communicates. It does not guarantee an AI answer's correctness.
Conversation storage is an application decision, not the API’s primary role.

title: JSON
goal: Read structured information and identify fields that matter.
meaning: JSON is a text format that stores data as named fields and values. Curly braces hold objects, while square brackets hold lists.
work: A support request returns an error object. You locate fields such as status, message and request_id without confusing them with sensitive authentication details.
look: Field names, their values, nesting, missing required fields and unexpected data types.
mistake: Confusing the text name of a field with the value it contains, or pasting secret tokens into a support ticket.
q: Which field can help engineering trace this example request?
options: request_id
status without its associated request
the visible wording alone
why: The request_id identifies the specific request to investigate. Keep the sample ID fictional in public practice.
optionReasons: The request_id identifies the specific request to investigate. Keep the sample ID fictional in public practice.
A status describes the outcome but does not uniquely trace this request.
Wording alone does not identify the request across components.

title: HTTP
goal: Recognize response code categories and select useful next checks.
meaning: HTTP is the protocol commonly used for web requests. Status codes indicate the type of result: 2xx success, 4xx request-side issues, and 5xx server-side failures.
work: An AI customer sees HTTP 429. You investigate rate limits and request volume before recommending a retry strategy.
look: Exact status code, provider error text, retry guidance, and whether the error repeats across accounts.
mistake: Treating a status code as conclusive proof of one exact root cause.
q: What should you investigate first for HTTP 429?
options: Increase retries immediately to restore the service
Check volume, limits and Retry-After guidance
Replace the API key before checking usage
why: 429 usually indicates rate limiting. Check usage, limits and any Retry-After response guidance.
optionReasons: Immediate repeated retries can worsen rate limiting.
429 usually indicates rate limiting. Check usage, limits and any Retry-After response guidance.
The log does not provide evidence of rejected authentication.

title: Logs
goal: Find timestamps, request IDs, status codes and error messages.
meaning: Logs are records of software events. They help reconstruct what happened, when it happened, and which component reported the event.
work: A customer says chat stopped at 10:30. You correlate a timestamp and request ID with relevant errors.
look: Time and timezone, request ID, status code, error message, environment and event sequence.
mistake: Reading one log line without context, or sharing raw logs containing sensitive personal information.
example:
10:30:01 request received  id=req-demo-88
10:30:02 model call started id=req-demo-88
10:30:03 HTTP 503         id=req-demo-88
q: Why is a request ID useful?
options: It confirms all events have the same cause
It helps correlate events from the same request
It proves the user saw the returned response
why: Request IDs help correlate records across services. They are evidence, not a fix.
optionReasons: Correlation does not establish a shared root cause.
Request IDs help correlate records across services. They are evidence, not a fix.
A request ID does not prove the client displayed the response.

title: Troubleshooting
goal: Investigate issues methodically instead of guessing.
meaning: Troubleshooting means describing a problem, gathering evidence, testing explanations and deciding the safest next action.
work: An AI assistant fails for one account. You reproduce the issue with a safe test, compare other accounts, examine logs and narrow possible causes.
look: Who is affected, first observed time, recent changes, reproduction steps, logs and what has already been tried.
mistake: Changing many settings at once, or declaring a root cause before the evidence supports it.
example:
1. Understand → 2. Reproduce → 3. Inspect
4. Investigate → 5. Escalate → 6. Communicate
q: What should happen before deciding the root cause?
options: Gather evidence and compare possible explanations
Change several settings to see what works
Confirm a cause from the first error line
why: Good troubleshooting starts with evidence. A plausible guess is not yet a confirmed diagnosis.
optionReasons: Good troubleshooting starts with evidence. A plausible guess is not yet a confirmed diagnosis.
Several changes at once make it harder to identify which one mattered.
A first error line needs context before it becomes a confirmed diagnosis.

title: Support tickets
goal: Write clear handovers that help technical colleagues act.
meaning: A support ticket is a structured record of a reported issue, its impact, the evidence collected and the assistance needed.
work: You send engineering a ticket with issue scope, exact error, timestamps, reproduction steps and a clear investigation request.
look: Summary, impact, environment, reproduction steps, expected versus actual result, request ID, and next action.
mistake: Writing only 'AI broken' or adding unsupported conclusions as facts.
example:
Summary: Chat requests fail
Impact: One test account
Status: HTTP 429
Request ID: req-demo-4721
Next step: Verify the account's rate limits
q: Which ticket is most helpful to an engineer?
options: Chat is failing; the backend must be broken
The model is unavailable; no evidence collected yet
One test account gets HTTP 429; time and request ID attached
why: Specific scope and verifiable evidence make a ticket actionable.
optionReasons: This assumes a backend cause without supporting evidence.
This declares a model cause without documenting what was observed.
Specific scope and verifiable evidence make a ticket actionable.

title: AI model behavior
goal: Recognize hallucinations, limitations and unexpected outputs.
meaning: AI models can produce fluent answers that are incomplete, incorrect or inconsistent. Hallucination means generated information that is not grounded in reliable evidence.
work: An AI assistant invents an account feature. You compare its answer with the approved documentation and reproduce the prompt before escalating.
look: Model and version, relevant prompt context, source evidence, reproducibility, safety boundaries and expected output.
mistake: Assuming a confident answer is always true, or exposing sensitive customer data to an unapproved model.
example:
Customer: Does this plan support feature X?
AI: Yes, always.
Documentation: Feature X is not listed.
Action: Verify against an authoritative source.
q: What is a responsible response to a confident but unsupported AI answer?
options: Use it if two generations agree
Compare the claim with an authoritative source
Change the wording before sharing the claim
why: Confidence is not accuracy. Verify important claims against trusted documentation or data.
optionReasons: Repeated agreement is not independent evidence.
Confidence is not accuracy. Verify important claims against trusted documentation or data.
Rewording a claim does not verify its accuracy.

title: Customer communication
goal: Give accurate, calm and professional updates.
meaning: Good customer communication acknowledges the issue, separates facts from assumptions and explains the next step without making unsupported promises.
work: A customer asks if the outage is fixed. You report what is confirmed and explain how the investigation will continue.
look: Clear acknowledgement, verified facts, a realistic next action, ownership and respectful wording.
mistake: Promising a fix or deadline without confirmation, or overwhelming the customer with internal jargon.
example: Thank you for reporting this. We have confirmed failed requests and are investigating the cause. We will share the next update when we have verified the next steps.
options: The provider is responsible; we expect it fixed shortly
We are reviewing failed requests and will share confirmed findings
Please retry repeatedly while we investigate
why: The best update shares verified observations, explains the next step and avoids false promises.
optionReasons: The cause and expected fix are not established.
The best update shares verified observations, explains the next step and avoids false promises.
Uncontrolled repeated retries can duplicate work or increase load.
